strengths: Provides a useful and well-motivated empirical analysis of global attention sparsity in VGGT and π³, showing that probability mass concentrates on a small subset of patch-patch interactions that correspond to geometrically meaningful cross-view matches, and that mid-stack layers carry the key cross-view integration (supported by a layer-drop ablation).

The proposed method is training-free and does not require retraining or modification of the backbone, which makes it practical and easy to adopt; the observation that special tokens (camera/register) must be treated separately from patch tokens is a sensible design choice validated by an ablation (Fig. A-1).

Evaluation breadth is strong: relative pose estimation (Real Estate 10K, CO3Dv2, TUM, ScanNet), multi-view reconstruction (7Scenes, NRGBD, DTU, ETH3D), and scene-level pose estimation (Tanks & Temples) with multiple input sizes, plus full result tables in the supplement.

Results demonstrate that multi-view reconstruction (Chamfer distance, ATE) is quite robust to sparsification even at high sparsity ratios, and the method yields real speedups (roughly 3–3.4× end-to-end at ~75% sparsity on large frame counts), addressing a genuine scalability bottleneck in VGGT.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is limited. The core block-sparse attention kernel is essentially adopted from SparseAttention [39]; the paper's own contributions are the sparsity analysis and the special-token handling, which are incremental. The abstract/discussion acknowledge the kernel is reused, but no direct comparison against SparseAttention (or other sparse/efficient attention baselines) is provided, so the marginal benefit of the proposed adaptations over the off-the-shelf method is not quantified.

The central claim of 'up to 4× faster inference with comparable task performance' is overstated. Pose estimation degrades substantially at high sparsity (e.g., Table 1: VGGT RRA@5 drops from 84.4 to 56.9 and RTA@5 from 81.5 to 65.6 at 75% sparsity; Real Estate 10K AUC@30 falls markedly in Fig. 7), so 'comparable' performance does not hold at the 4× operating point. The results that are robust are largely reconstruction metrics, not pose.

The reported '4×' speedup conflates global-attention speedup with end-to-end speedup. By the paper's own discussion and Fig. 1, global attention is only part of the runtime, so end-to-end speedup is bounded (Amdahl), and Table 1 shows ~3.3–3.4× end-to-end at best. Presenting '4× faster inference' in the abstract without this qualification is misleading.

Speedups only materialize at large frame counts. At 25 frames (Table 1) VGGT-S25 is slightly slower than dense VGGT (0.66s vs 0.63s), and the overhead of pooled Q/K computation and mask selection is not analyzed or reported, leaving unclear when the method is actually beneficial.

The mask-prediction design (average-pooled Q/K similarity with CDF threshold τ and top-k ratio ρ) involves hyperparameters whose sensitivity is not thoroughly explored; the paper fixes a block size of 128/64 for the trained variant but does not report how block size affects the accuracy/efficiency trade-off in the training-free setting.

No comparison to other efficient-attention alternatives that could serve as baselines (e.g., linear attention, other sparse patterns, token merging) is given, so it is difficult to judge whether block-sparse attention is the best choice for this problem.

strengths: Addresses a timely and practically important problem: the quadratic global-attention cost that makes VGGT/π³ hard to scale to large image collections, with a training-free retrofit that does not require retraining the backbone.

The empirical analysis of VGGT's global attention is a genuinely useful characterization: the sparsity visualization (Fig. 3, 4), the per-layer statistics (S2S/S2P/P2P/P2S), and the layer-drop ablation (Fig. 5, Fig. A-3) provide a plausible and interesting account of where cross-view information is integrated, and are well supported by the supplementary material.

The method is simple and portable: the binary block mask is kernel-agnostic and can in principle be dropped onto any standard block-sparse attention kernel, and the approach is demonstrated on two different models (VGGT and π³).

Evaluation breadth is good: nine benchmarks spanning relative pose and pointmap estimation (Real Estate 10K, CO3Dv2, TUM, ScanNet, 7Scenes, NRGBD, DTU, ETH3D) plus scene-level pose on Tanks & Temples at multiple frame counts, with full result tables in the supplement.

The supplementary ablations are informative, in particular the demonstration that treating special (camera/register) tokens densely is important at high sparsity (Fig. A-1) and that learned projections do not help (Fig. A-2).
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty. The mask-prediction procedure (average-pool queries and keys, compute pooled similarity, apply top-k and CDF thresholding) is taken directly from SparseAttention [39], and the paper itself states the block-sparse implementation is independent of this work and could be built on top of FlashAttention. The net new contributions reduce to the sparsity analysis and the special-token handling, which is a thin delta for a top-tier venue.

The headline claims are overstated relative to the evidence. The abstract promises 'up to 4× faster inference with comparable task performance,' but the 4× figure is attention-only; measured end-to-end speedups are roughly 2× at realistic settings (e.g., Tanks & Temples full 35 s → 17.9 s; 200 frames 18 s → 8.5 s), and accuracy degrades materially at those settings (Real Estate RRA@5 84.8 → 81.4 at S50; CO3Dv2 AUC@30 0.908 → 0.896; π³ also drops). This is a genuine speed–accuracy trade-off, not 'matched' or 'comparable' performance.

There is no recommended operating point that preserves accuracy at a meaningful speedup; the paper only presents trade-off curves while sweeping top-k and the CDF threshold, so the practical deployment recipe (how to fix these hyperparameters for a new scene) is unclear.

Timing accounting is incomplete and potentially favorable to the method: end-to-end numbers are given only for one benchmark, and the cost of the mask-prediction stage (pooling, pooled QK^T, top-k/CDF selection) is not separated from the attention speedup, even though that overhead is part of the proposed pipeline.

The comparison in Fig. 7 places horizontal dashed constants for Fast3r, CUT3R, and FLARE against the sparsified models, but these are not evaluated under matched conditions (frame counts, resolution, protocol), so the claim that the sparse models are 'on par or better than other state-of-the-art methods' is weakly supported. The more meaningful comparison against VGGT itself shows consistent degradation.

The core observation that softmax attention is sparse/peaked is largely expected, and the interpretation that highly activated entries correspond to geometric matches is supported only qualitatively (Fig. 4 left, Fig. A-6), not quantitatively.
No code or reproducibility artifact is referenced, and several implementation details (block sizes, threshold selection) appear only in the supplement, limiting reproducibility.

strengths: Addresses a real and clearly motivated bottleneck: the quadratic cost of VGGT's global attention layers, which limits scalability to large image collections. The runtime breakdown in Fig. 1 makes the problem concrete.

The empirical analysis of attention patterns is the strongest part of the paper. Figures 3 and 4 show that global attention is highly sparse and that patch-to-patch interactions dominate the variation, and the layer-drop ablation in Fig. 5 (with full results in Supp. Fig. A-3) gives a non-obvious insight that middle aggregator layers carry the essential cross-view information. This is a genuinely useful characterization of VGGT/π³.

The method is training-free, kernel-agnostic, and requires no changes to encoders or task heads, which makes it practically attractive and easy to adopt. It is demonstrated on two different models (VGGT and π³), supporting the generality claim.

Evaluation breadth is good: relative pose (Real Estate 10K, CO3Dv2), reconstruction (7Scenes, NRGBD, DTU, ETH3D), SLAM-style pose (TUM, ScanNet), and scene-level pose (Tanks & Temples), with full per-configuration tables in the supplement (Tables A-1 to A-13).

The ablations are honest and informative: Supp. A.1 shows that keeping special tokens dense is important at high sparsity, and Supp. A.2 reports a negative result that learned linear mask predictors do not beat the training-free pooling baseline.
The special-token handling (splitting patch tokens from camera/register tokens and computing full attention on the latter) is a sensible design choice that is properly ablated rather than asserted.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate. The core mechanism is adopted from SpA 3 (Zhang et al., ICLR 2025), and the mask-prediction strategy (average-pooled query/key similarity to score blocks) is closely related to existing training-free sparse-attention work such as SeerAttention and SpargeAttn, which the authors themselves cite. The paper's own novelty is largely the application to VGGT/π³ plus the analysis and the special-token treatment, not a new sparse-attention formulation.

The headline claim of 'up to 4× faster inference with comparable task performance' (Abstract) is misleading. Table 1 shows end-to-end speedups are far smaller at the sparsity levels where accuracy is preserved: at 200 frames, VGGT-S25 is 17.9s vs 18s baseline (≈1.0×), and S50 is 8.5s (≈2.1×); at 25 frames S25 (0.66s) is actually slower than the 0.63s baseline. The 4× figure is a theoretical bound on the global-attention sub-component (1/(1−ρ)) and is only approached at S75, where accuracy collapses (e.g., Tanks & Temples full: RRA@5 46.0 vs 73.4).

The 'on par with the original model' claim holds only in a narrow moderate-sparsity band. Tables A-1 to A-13 show pronounced degradation at higher sparsity on several benchmarks (e.g., DTU and ETH3D Chamfer distance, NRGBD), yet the main-text Fig. 7 emphasizes graceful degradation. The trade-off is real but presented more favorably than the numbers support.

Fig. 7 plots the sparse models against Fast3R, CUT3R, and FLARE but does not show the dense VGGT/π³ baseline on the same axes, making it hard to judge how much accuracy is lost relative to the unsparsified model that the paper is trying to match. The dense baseline is only recoverable by cross-referencing the supplementary tables.

Key hyperparameters of the method are not stated in the main text. The block size b, the default CDF threshold τ, and the sparse ratio ρ used for the headline results are only reported per-row in the tables (and block size only in Supp. A.2). This hinders reproducibility and makes it unclear how a practitioner would choose these values.

The paper claims kernel-agnosticism and hardware-friendliness but does not report attention-kernel-level timing or memory measurements, despite motivating the work with the 35GB attention-matrix figure. The only timing evidence is end-to-end (Table 1), which conflates kernel efficiency with mask-prediction overhead; the near-zero speedup at S25 suggests the overhead is significant and deserves explicit analysis.

Some reported effects are unexplained: sparse variants occasionally outperform the dense model at low sparsity (e.g., TUM/ScanNet in Fig. 7), which is not discussed and could indicate run-to-run variance or a regularization effect rather than genuine improvement.

strengths: The paper provides a well-motivated empirical analysis of attention sparsity in multi-view geometry transformers (VGGT, π³, MapAnything), showing that probability mass concentrates on a small subset of patch-patch interactions that correspond to cross-view geometric correspondences, and that mid-aggregator layers carry the bulk of cross-view integration. This analysis is novel and practically useful.

The proposed block-sparse global attention is training-free and decoupled from model weights, and it is shown to integrate seamlessly into three architecturally distinct models (VGGT, π³, MapAnything) with no retraining, which strengthens the generality claim.

The experimental suite is broad, covering relative pose estimation (Real Estate 10K, CO3Dv2, TUM, ScanNet), pointmap estimation (7Scenes, NRGBD, DTU, ETH3D), and long-sequence Tanks & Temples, plus ablations against SpargeAttention and random masking. The sparsity-accuracy trade-off curves (Fig. 7, 9, 10) support the central claim of comparable task performance with substantial compute savings.

The design choices are well-justified and supported by ablation: combining CDF thresholding with a top-k sparsity floor is shown to be more robust than either mechanism alone, and treating special tokens (camera/register) densely is demonstrated to be necessary at high sparsity (Fig. A-2). The theoretical FLOPs analysis (Tab. A-1) and the long-sequence results (Fig. A-1) provide additional supporting evidence for scalability.
The paper is generally clearly written, with informative figures (attention-map visualizations, layer-drop ablations) and a thorough supplement with full result tables, which aids reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core sparse-attention mechanism is heavily derivative of SpargeAttention; the contribution is largely an adaptation (dropping Hilbert permutation and self-similarity filtering, adding a top-k/CDF combination) rather than a fundamentally new method. Novelty is moderate.

The reported 'effective sparsity ratios' in the main-text plots are far lower than the numbers in the supplement tables (e.g., 75% claimed vs. effective sparsity often 40-60% on Real Estate 10K/CO3Dv2). This discrepancy makes it harder to judge the actual compute savings achieved at the claimed operating points, and the headline '3×' speedup is for global attention only, not end-to-end. The paper acknowledges this but does not present clean end-to-end latency measurements per model/benchmark.

Performance degradation at high sparsity is non-trivial and varies significantly across models and datasets (e.g., MapAnything on CO3Dv2 shows a marked AUC@30 drop, and the paper even notes that apparent ETH3D improvements are 'likely attributable to randomness'). This weakens the general claim of 'comparable task performance' and suggests the method's robustness is somewhat model- and task-dependent.

The comparison does not include training-based sparse-attention or token-pruning baselines (the SeerAttention-style trained projection is relegated to appendix and shows no gain, but other families are not compared), and there is no evaluation of the method's behavior at higher input resolution, despite the discussion noting resolution as a key bottleneck.

Some claims rely on qualitative evidence (Fig. 8, A-6) that is hard to verify quantitatively, and the attribution of mid-layer importance focuses on VGGT while the MapAnything layer-skip behavior differs, leaving the analysis somewhat model-specific rather than a general principle.

strengths: Addresses a practically important bottleneck: global attention dominates runtime in feed-forward multi-view geometry transformers such as VGGT, pi3, and MapAnything.
Provides useful empirical analysis of VGGT's global attention, including visualizations showing concentrated attention and layer-drop ablations suggesting mid-aggregator layers are critical.
The proposed training-free adaptation is easy to integrate in principle and avoids retraining or extra annotations; keeping special-token interactions dense is a sensible design choice.
Evaluates on a broad set of multi-view benchmarks (Co3Dv2, Real Estate 10K, TUM, ScanNet, 7Scenes, NRGBD, DTU, ETH3D, Tanks & Temples) and includes full result tables in the supplement.
Reports meaningful speedups on long sequences and demonstrates applicability to multiple architectures, which supports the practical relevance of the approach.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core mechanism is existing block-sparse attention (using the SpargeAttention kernel) with pooled query-key top-k/CDF block selection; the paper mostly adapts and simplifies existing sparse-attention components rather than proposing a fundamentally new method.

The central claims are overstated. The abstract advertises >3x acceleration while maintaining comparable task performance, but the experiments show continuous degradation, e.g. VGGT Co3Dv2 AUC@30 drops from 0.908 to 0.795 at ~75% sparsity, and pi3/MapAnything show larger drops on several benchmarks. End-to-end speedups are ~1.5x at 100 frames and ~2x at 200-300 frames, with up to 3x only on much longer sequences. MapAnything timing is additionally described as inaccurate due to pre/post-processing, further weakening the speed claims.

Accuracy preservation is not convincingly demonstrated. Many tables lack direct dense-baseline rows, and the main text mostly shows aggregated trade-off plots rather than precise numerical comparisons against the original models. The claim of being on par is often supported only by comparison to other state-of-the-art methods, not to the unmodified model at matched settings.

There is a disconnect between the analysis and the method. The layer-drop ablation argues that middle aggregator layers are especially important, but the proposed approach applies block-sparse attention across global layers rather than explicitly preserving or adaptively densifying critical mid-layers; the paper does not provide per-layer sparsity/accuracy analysis to justify this.

The theoretical FLOP analysis is flawed or at least unclear. Eq. 6 appears to omit the number of global attention blocks L_G (and mixes token count T/t), so the theoretical speedup table in the supplement is not reliable. The overhead of mask prediction (pooling, softmax, top-k/CDF selection) is also not accounted for in speedup estimates.

Reproducibility is limited: no code release is mentioned, key implementation details such as block sizes, exact tau/rho schedules, kernel integration details, and wall-clock measurement protocol are incomplete or relegated to the supplement. The claim that the method is kernel-agnostic is not demonstrated beyond the chosen SpargeAttention kernel.

Baselines and ablations are insufficient for the strength of the claims. The main text compares mainly to random masking and SpargeAttention, without evaluating simple alternatives such as local/window attention, frame subsampling, or reduced resolution under matched runtime. Mask recall against true attention mass is not quantified, so the reliability of the sparse block prediction remains unclear.

Evaluation inconsistencies make cross-model conclusions less solid. Some benchmarks use subsets or custom sampling (e.g., every second ScanNet sequence, 90 frames with stride 3, limited Tanks & Temples frame counts), and MapAnything degrades substantially at higher sparsity, which weakens the generality claim.

strengths: Addresses an important bottleneck in multi-view geometry transformers: the quadratic complexity of global attention dominates runtime as the number of frames grows, shown in Fig. 1; the proposed method targets this directly with a training-free sparse attention scheme.

Comprehensive empirical analysis: visualizations of attention maps (Figs. 3-4 and A-8-A-10) reveal strong sparsity concentrated in patch-patch interactions and mid-layer importance; this motivates the method and is supported by layer-drop ablations.

Broad evaluation and strong empirical results: integrates into VGGT, pi3, and MapAnything; experiments cover multiple benchmarks (Real Estate 10K, CO3Dv2, TUM, ScanNet, 7Scenes, NRGBD, DTU, ETH3D, Tanks & Temples) with pose estimation, pointmap estimation, and long-sequence tests; the efficiency-accuracy trade-offs are favorable (Figs. 7-9; Tables A-2 to A-16).

Practical and reproducible design: training-free, no backward passes, kernel-agnostic, and decoupled from hardware-specific optimizations; ablations compare random masking, SpargeAttention, CDF-only, special-token handling, and learned projections.

Good clarity and supplementary detail: theoretical FLOPs analysis, long-sequence experiments, and complete quantitative tables help substantiate claims; limitations and future directions (higher resolution, integration with FlashAttention) are discussed.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat limited: the method builds heavily on existing block-sparse attention and specifically reuses the SpargeAttention kernel, with main modifications (combined CDF+top-k thresholding, special-token separation, omission of Hilbert permutation) being relatively incremental.

Block-mask prediction via average-pooled query/key similarity is heuristic; while ablations compare learned projections with no improvement, there is no theoretical guarantee that this low-resolution approximation preserves the necessary attention mass across diverse scenes/models.

Hyperparameter sensitivity is not fully resolved: the CDF threshold, sparsity ratio, and block size are user-set; although the paper sweeps sparsity levels, it does not provide an automatic selection rule or analyze failure cases where dense attention might be required.

Efficiency comparisons rely on the original dense models as baselines; the paper does not compare against other efficiency strategies (e.g., quantization, distillation, token pruning, or alternative sparse attention kernels) for multi-view geometry, so the relative advantage over possible alternatives is not fully established.

Reproducibility details are limited regarding exact kernel-level integration and hardware measurements; no code release is mentioned, and runtime measurements may depend on implementation details, GPU, and pre/post-processing overhead, especially for MapAnything.

Attention sparsity is analyzed primarily on VGGT layer 15 and related models; generalization to very high-resolution inputs or other transformer-based geometry estimators is proposed but not demonstrated in the main text.
